title: Build a Private IT Help Desk with IIS
description: Learn IIS by building, protecting and recovering a real osTicket help desk on APP01.
baseline: VMware Workstation Pro · Windows Server 2019 APP01 · lab.example.test · IIS + PHP 8.4.27 minimum / newer patched 8.4 x64 NTS + maintained MariaDB 10.11 · osTicket self-hosted edition
prerequisite: Let’s give your Windows server a useful job. We’ll build a help desk where a practice user can report a problem and an IT agent can resolve it. Start after the APP01 domain-join and IIS foundation lesson; each class below adds one small piece.
supplies: A prepared APP01 member VM and a private Windows client; do not install the app on DC01/DC02.
Working lab.example.test AD DNS and the actual private IPs from your lab plan.
Administrator rights on your own lab VMs, trusted installers and a password manager.
An your practice mailbox only if you choose the optional mail integration class.
A recovery plan and protected backup space outside the website folder.

steps.title: Meet the machines
steps.where: VMware Workstation Pro on your host
actions: In VMware Workstation Pro, double-click APP01 in Library. Sign in to its Windows Server desktop. APP01 is our fictional application server name; use your recorded name if it differs.
Write APP01 = private application server. It will host IIS, PHP and osTicket. In this small practice build, MariaDB also runs locally on APP01 and listens only to local application connections.
Write DC01 and DC02 = directory and DNS servers. They help computers sign in and find names; we do not install the ticketing website on them.
Write your actual APP01 IPv4 address, subnet and DNS addresses. The course example is APP01 at 10.50.0.30, with DC01 at 10.50.0.10. These values must match your earlier network build.

For a fresh build, use lab.example.test as the private domain and helpdesk.lab.example.test as the website name. These are made-up training names; no public DNS purchase or router port forward is needed.

Leave this application private for this class. In the later DMZ class, a separate gateway receives visitor requests and only forwards the approved web connection to private IIS. A gateway is not where the database or domain controllers belong.
steps.expected: You have a short machine and address list.

steps.title: Collect the installers and recovery point
steps.where: APP01 · browser and your backup notes
actions: Get the free self-hosted osTicket package from osticket.com/download. For PHP, open https://www.php.net/downloads.php → Windows downloads → PHP 8.4 → x64 Non Thread Safe → Zip. Choose the runtime ZIP, not the source, debug pack or development SDK. Check the ZIP filename/version and compare its SHA-256 with the value on the official download page. Save the trusted ZIP and version record outside the website folder.
Also obtain Microsoft Visual C++ 2015–2022 x64 Redistributable and Microsoft IIS URL Rewrite 2.1 from their official sites. Avoid old all-in-one tutorial bundles and retired Web Platform Installer.
Record the exact versions. Back up APP01 before changes; a short-lived VMware checkpoint of this practice member VM is a convenience, not a database backup and never an AD recovery recipe.

steps.title: Unpack and configure PHP
steps.where: APP01 · File Explorer and Notepad as administrator
actions: For a fresh install, use the official PHP 8.4 x64 Non Thread Safe runtime ZIP, version 8.4.27 or a newer patched 8.4 release. Install Microsoft Visual C++ x64 Redistributable. Right-click the ZIP → Extract All; put its contents directly in C:\PHP, so C:\PHP\php-cgi.exe exists. If C:\PHP already contains a working runtime, do not overwrite it: use the later Update PHP and Recover Safely class instead.

Copy php.ini-production to php.ini. Open php.ini and set extension_dir="C:\PHP\ext". Enable the supplied mysqli, mbstring, intl, gd and fileinfo extensions by removing their leading semicolons. Enable openssl if supplied and needed for TLS mail. Do not download random extension DLLs.
Set date.timezone="UTC", log_errors=On, display_errors=Off and cgi.fix_pathinfo=1. Keep PHP files outside the website root. Save and run the checks.

Also set session.save_path="C:\Sites\HelpdeskRuntime\sessions", upload_tmp_dir="C:\Sites\HelpdeskRuntime\uploads" and error_log="C:\Sites\HelpdeskRuntime\php-errors.log". We will create and permission those private runtime folders when we create the pool.
steps.expected: The selected 8.4 runtime is at least 8.4.27, its published ZIP hash matches, and the required extensions load without warnings.

screenshot.title: Unpack and configure PHP
screenshot.instructions: Compare the named controls with your screen. Use the fictional practice values in the written actions.

steps.title: Add the FastCGI handler
steps.where: APP01 · IIS Manager → APP01 → Handler Mappings
actions: Choose Add Module Mapping. Request path: *.php. Module: FastCgiModule. Executable: C:\PHP\php-cgi.exe. Name: PHP-FastCGI.
Choose OK and Yes when asked to create a FastCGI application. If FastCgiModule is absent, return to the CGI role check.
Use php-cgi.exe, not php.exe. Keep Enable 32-Bit Applications=False for an x64 PHP pool.
steps.expected: IIS has a PHP-FastCGI mapping to the x64 CGI executable.

screenshot.title: Add the FastCGI handler
screenshot.instructions: Compare the named controls with your screen. Use the fictional practice values in the written actions.

steps.title: Prove PHP runs and remove the test
steps.where: APP01 · elevated PowerShell and browser
actions: Write the temporary page below into the existing IIS root. It prints the PHP version and server interface actually serving the browser request; it does not publish a phpinfo dump.

Open http://localhost/php-check.php on APP01. Check that the browser shows PHP 8.4.27 or a newer patched 8.4 release, followed by cgi-fcgi. If it shows an older version, a different runtime is still mapped in IIS. If PHP downloads or appears as source text, stop and fix the handler.
Remove the test file after checking. A successful command-line PHP test alone does not prove IIS can execute PHP.
steps.expected: The IIS-served page reports the required patched runtime and cgi-fcgi, and the temporary page is removed.
steps.command:
Set-Content -LiteralPath C:\inetpub\wwwroot\php-check.php -Value '<?php echo PHP_VERSION . " / " . PHP_SAPI; ?>' -Encoding ASCII
# After the browser check:
Remove-Item -LiteralPath C:\inetpub\wwwroot\php-check.php

steps.title: Create the pool and site
steps.where: APP01 · IIS Manager
actions: In Application Pools choose Add Application Pool. Name it PracticeHelpdesk, select No Managed Code and Integrated. Its identity stays ApplicationPoolIdentity.
Right-click Sites → Add Website. Site name: PracticeHelpdesk. Select the matching pool. Physical path: C:\Sites\PracticeHelpdesk.

steps.title: Grant limited file access
steps.where: APP01 · elevated Windows PowerShell
actions: Grant the pool Read and Execute on the website folder. Grant Modify on ost-config.php only for the installer. Run the commands below.
In IIS Manager select PracticeHelpdesk → Authentication → Anonymous Authentication → Edit → Application pool identity. This makes anonymous requests use the named pool’s file rights.
In Default Document ensure index.php is present, adding it if necessary. Do not grant Everyone Full Control or make the whole site writable.

Create the private runtime folders in the command below and grant Modify only there to this pool. These folders stay outside the website root; they hold temporary uploads, sessions and the PHP error log.
steps.expected: The pool can read the app and temporarily write its configuration file.
steps.command:
icacls C:\Sites\PracticeHelpdesk /grant "IIS AppPool\PracticeHelpdesk:(OI)(CI)(RX)"
icacls C:\Sites\PracticeHelpdesk\include\ost-config.php /grant "IIS AppPool\PracticeHelpdesk:(M)"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path C:\Sites\HelpdeskRuntime\sessions,C:\Sites\HelpdeskRuntime\uploads
icacls C:\Sites\HelpdeskRuntime /grant "IIS AppPool\PracticeHelpdesk:(OI)(CI)(M)"

steps.title: Create the private DNS record
steps.where: DC01 · Server Manager → Tools → DNS
actions: Expand your DC → Forward Lookup Zones → lab.example.test. This should already be your AD-integrated zone from the domain build.
Right-click the zone → New Host (A or AAAA). Name: helpdesk. IP address: APP01’s recorded private IPv4 address. Choose Add Host.
Do not change the root lab.example.test record, registrar nameservers, MX records, or public DNS. Internal AD DNS must separately resolve any public services your clients need.
steps.expected: Private DNS maps helpdesk.lab.example.test to APP01, without changing public records.

steps.where: Private Windows lab client · PowerShell
actions: Confirm this client uses your AD DNS servers. Run Resolve-DnsName below and compare the returned IP to APP01.
A wrong answer usually means a stale record, wrong client DNS server or mismatched subnet. Correct that before opening the app.
Use the exact hostname in IIS bindings. Browsing by IP can select a different IIS site.

steps.title: Scope the web firewall access
steps.where: APP01 and your private lab client
actions: On APP01 open Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security. Check existing IIS inbound rules before adding another.

If no suitable rule exists: Inbound Rules → New Rule → Port → TCP → Specific local ports: 443 → Allow the connection → Domain profile → name Practice Helpdesk HTTPS. Open the new rule → Scope → Remote IP addresses → These IP addresses → Add your recorded lab subnet. Check other enabled 443 rules too; a broad allow rule can defeat this scope.

Allow TCP 443 only from your recorded lab subnet. If your practice setup needs HTTP temporarily, scope TCP 80 to that same subnet and remove the temporary allowance when HTTPS is ready. Do not open database port 3306.
From the client, test 443 after the next HTTPS lesson; before its binding exists, failure is expected. No router forwarding or public inbound RDP is needed.
steps.expected: You have a private-only web access plan; DNS resolution works.
steps.command:
# Run on the private client after HTTPS is configured:
Test-NetConnection helpdesk.lab.example.test -Port 443

steps.title: Trust and test on the practice client
steps.where: APP01 certlm.msc, then your disposable private Windows client
actions: On APP01 press Win+R → certlm.msc → Personal → Certificates. Open your certificate, check its name and thumbprint, then All Tasks → Export → No, do not export the private key → DER encoded .CER.

steps.title: Freeze changes and take a logical backup

actions: Tell practice users the desk is offline, set Helpdesk Status to Offline, then stop only the PracticeHelpdesk pool so no web writes occur during the backup.

Create a protected folder such as D:\LabBackups only if D: exists; otherwise choose another protected non-web folder. Run mariadb-dump from the installed MariaDB bin folder using --result-file. Never redirect binary or dump data through Windows PowerShell’s default text encoding.
The command prompts for the database administrator password. Confirm exit code 0, a nonempty SQL file and a backup record. Keep database access local.

If an attachments plugin stores files outside the database, include that exact location. Keep certificate private-key backups only in protected storage with a separate recovery process.

# Inside the MariaDB client on the isolated recovery VM:
SOURCE D:/LabBackups/osticket.sql;

lessons.title: Update PHP and Recover Safely
lessons.description: Stage a patched PHP runtime, test it on a restored copy, switch IIS and recover safely if a check fails.
lessons.what: Let’s practise a real PHP security update without overwriting the only working copy. We’ll keep a recovery record, test first and make one controlled switch.
lessons.why: An application can keep working on a vulnerable runtime. We need to prove both that the security fix is active in IIS and that the help desk still works.
needs: Complete Back Up and Restore the Help Desk first, including the isolated recovery test.
A verified PHP 8.4.27 or newer patched 8.4 x64 NTS ZIP, administrator access and a protected backup location.
A private test client, a practice restored APP01 copy and your actual ticket/attachment/mail acceptance checks.
bestPractices: Keep old and candidate PHP folders separate; verify hashes and matching extension builds.
Keep vulnerable PHP out of service even if the patched application needs troubleshooting.
Change only the target site/pool. Record shared FastCGI or environment required connections and services before touching them.
commonMistakes: Checking php.exe on PATH while IIS continues using another php-cgi.exe.
Copying old extension DLLs into a new PHP build or leaving extension_dir/PHPRC pointed at old files.
Rolling back into a vulnerable version and reopening it to users.
Restoring a whole database or all IIS sites to fix one handler mapping.

troubleshooting.problem: The browser still shows the old version.
troubleshooting.fix: Check this site’s PHP handler, the corresponding FastCGI full path/Arguments, PHPRC and the loaded php.ini. Stop and start the target pool; do not assume the CLI runtime is the web runtime.

troubleshooting.problem: The new runtime cannot load an extension.
troubleshooting.fix: Check the x64 NTS branch/build, its Visual C++ runtime, extension_dir and DLL dependencies. Keep the pool stopped until the candidate loads and passes tests.

lessons.pass: The actual IIS-served runtime is security-approved and all application checks pass, or the service remains unavailable with a documented safe recovery decision.
lessons.exercise: On an isolated restored copy, practise switching between two security-approved candidate folders and record how you would keep a vulnerable previous runtime offline. Do not install or expose an unpatched runtime just to demonstrate the failure.

quiz.question: The old PHP build works but is below the fixed security minimum. What is the safe rollback decision?
options: Keep the service unavailable and repair a patched candidate or recover on an isolated copy.
Reopen the old build because the login page works.
quiz.explanation: A functional but vulnerable runtime is not an acceptable live recovery state.

quiz.question: Which check proves IIS is actually using the patched runtime?
options: A temporary private page reporting PHP_VERSION, PHP_SAPI and its loaded INI, followed by removal.
quiz.explanation: The browser request checks the runtime serving that website; CLI tools can point to another installation.

steps.title: Record what IIS is really using
steps.where: APP01 · IIS Manager and a private browser
actions: Finish the Backup and Restore class first. Tell practice users that you are planning maintenance. This PHP-only update does not include an osTicket upgrade or database schema change.

In IIS Manager select Sites → PracticeHelpdesk → Handler Mappings → PHP-FastCGI → Edit. Record the exact php-cgi.exe path. At the server node open FastCGI Settings and record that same executable, its Arguments and Environment Variables. Check PHPRC or PHP_INI_SCAN_DIR if present: either can load configuration from another folder.

Use a short-lived PHP version page in this private site to record PHP_VERSION, PHP_SAPI and php_ini_loaded_file(). Remove it after checking. Also record the ticket number, attachment and mail test you will repeat after the change.
If the running version is below the fixed minimum, stop the PracticeHelpdesk pool now and keep it unavailable until patched. A private address, HTTPS or IIS does not patch PHP.
steps.expected: Your change record names the current executable, actual web-served version, configuration path and acceptance checks.

screenshot.title: Record what IIS is really using
screenshot.instructions: Compare the written actions with your own practice machine. Diagrams are not screenshots or evidence of success.

steps.title: Protect the app before changing PHP
steps.where: APP01 · protected backups and elevated Windows PowerShell
actions: Create the tested database/files backup from Backup and Restore the Help Desk. Copy the current PHP folder, php.ini and any additional INI files to protected storage outside the web root. Record extensions, VC++ runtime, pool identity, runtime-folder ACLs and the existing handler/FastCGI settings.

Run the IIS configuration backup below. Record its generated name. This backup covers server configuration; restoring it blindly can change other websites. Our first rollback choice will be restoring only this site’s recorded PHP mapping.

Set the help desk Offline, stop PracticeHelpdesk and keep new tickets paused. If you use a temporary VMware checkpoint on this practice member server, record it as an additional recovery aid, not a substitute for the tested database/files backup. Never use this as a domain-controller recovery method.
steps.command:
Import-Module WebAdministration
$phpChangeTag = Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMdd-HHmmss'
& "$env:windir\System32\inetsrv\appcmd.exe" add backup "Practice-PHP-$phpChangeTag"
Stop-WebAppPool -Name 'PracticeHelpdesk'
Get-WebAppPoolState -Name 'PracticeHelpdesk'
steps.expected: A tested recovery package and exact pre-change mapping exist, with writes paused and the pool stopped.

screenshot.title: Protect the app before changing PHP
screenshot.instructions: Compare the written actions with your own practice machine. Diagrams are not screenshots or evidence of success.

steps.title: Download and stage the fixed runtime
steps.where: APP01 · browser, File Explorer and PowerShell
actions: Open https://www.php.net/downloads.php → Windows downloads → PHP 8.4 → x64 Non Thread Safe → Zip. The October 21 fixes begin at 8.4.27. Use a newer patched 8.4 release if one is available and compatible; do not switch major/minor branches merely to get a larger number.
Compare Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 on the actual downloaded ZIP with its official published SHA-256 before extracting. A matching filename alone does not check a download.
Extract into a NEW folder, for example C:\PHP-8.4.27. If your downloaded version is newer, use that version in the folder name and in every following path. Keep the previous runtime intact.

Start from the new package’s php.ini-production. Reapply the recorded settings deliberately. Point extension_dir to this new folder’s ext directory and keep session/upload/log paths on the existing protected runtime folders. Use only matching x64 NTS extensions built for this PHP branch; do not copy old DLLs wholesale.
Run the candidate checks below. Read any missing-runtime or extension warnings before proceeding.
steps.expected: A separate candidate folder contains a verified supported patched runtime, matching extensions and the intended configuration.

screenshot.title: Download and stage the fixed runtime
screenshot.instructions: Compare the written actions with your own practice machine. Diagrams are not screenshots or evidence of success.

steps.title: Try the update on an isolated copy first
steps.where: Isolated restored APP01 copy and a private test client
actions: Use your tested restore to build a separate copy. Keep the original APP01 protected, outgoing mail disabled on the copy and shared DNS unchanged. Use an isolated client’s temporary hosts entry for helpdesk.lab.example.test to reach only this test copy.

On the copy, map this site’s PHP handler and corresponding FastCGI application to the staged candidate, as described in the next step. Adjust PHPRC/PHP_INI_SCAN_DIR only for this app if they point to an old configuration. A shared global variable requires a separate impact review; do not change other apps silently.

Start the copy’s pool. Verify the web-served version, staff login, a fake ticket, a reply, attachment upload/download and the PHP/IIS error logs. Keep real outgoing mail disabled; record that mail still needs its live acceptance check.
If any test fails, stop here. Fix the candidate configuration or obtain a supported fix. Remove the isolated client’s temporary hosts entry after the pilot.
steps.expected: The isolated copy passes the recorded application checks on the patched candidate. No shared DNS was changed.

screenshot.title: Try the update on an isolated copy first
screenshot.instructions: Compare the written actions with your own practice machine. Diagrams are not screenshots or evidence of success.

steps.title: Switch only the Practice PHP mapping
steps.where: APP01 · IIS Manager with PracticeHelpdesk stopped
actions: At the server node open FastCGI Settings → Add Application. Full Path: C:\PHP-8.4.27\php-cgi.exe, or your recorded newer candidate. Reapply necessary non-secret FastCGI settings and app-specific environment variables to that candidate entry. Leave an old entry intact if another application still uses it.

Select Sites → PracticeHelpdesk → Handler Mappings → PHP-FastCGI → Edit. Change Executable to the same candidate php-cgi.exe path, leaving FastCgiModule and *.php unchanged. Confirm any creation prompt, and check FastCGI Settings again so the full path and Arguments match.

If PHPRC was configured, verify this app now loads the intended new php.ini. Ensure the pool identity has Read/Execute on the candidate folder, and retains Modify only on the private session/upload/log folders. Do not grant write access to all PHP binaries.
Start only PracticeHelpdesk using the command below. Stopping and starting the pool retires its old PHP workers. Do not use a server-wide iisreset for this single-app exercise.
steps.expected: Only the intended site points to the candidate, and its pool has restarted.

screenshot.title: Switch only the Practice PHP mapping
screenshot.instructions: Compare the written actions with your own practice machine. Diagrams are not screenshots or evidence of success.

steps.title: Check the web runtime and reopen carefully
steps.where: Private client → helpdesk.lab.example.test; APP01 logs
actions: On APP01 create the temporary version-check file below in this site’s physical root. From your private client open https://helpdesk.lab.example.test/php-version-check.php. Compare its version, cgi-fcgi SAPI and loaded php.ini path with your candidate. CLI output alone is not enough.

Require at least 8.4.27 on the supported 8.4 branch and review current PHP advisories for any newer security floor. If the page still reports the old runtime or wrong configuration, keep the site unavailable and check the site mapping, candidate FastCGI entry and environment variables.

Remove the temporary file, set the help desk Online for your practice client and repeat login, known ticket lookup, new ticket, reply, attachment and configured mail checks. Review new IIS/PHP errors. If an acceptance check fails, stop the pool and follow the rollback decision; do not leave a broken or vulnerable site serving.
Record the new runtime, test results and time. If the checks pass, reopen normal practice access, monitor errors and keep the protected previous configuration until the agreed retention period ends.
steps.command:
Set-Content -LiteralPath 'C:\Sites\PracticeHelpdesk\php-version-check.php' -Value '<?php echo PHP_VERSION . " / " . PHP_SAPI . " / " . php_ini_loaded_file(); ?>' -Encoding ASCII
# After verifying in the private browser, remove the temporary page:
Remove-Item -LiteralPath 'C:\Sites\PracticeHelpdesk\php-version-check.php'
steps.expected: The actual website uses the patched candidate, acceptance checks pass and the temporary page is gone.

screenshot.title: Check the web runtime and reopen carefully
screenshot.instructions: Compare the written actions with your own practice machine. Diagrams are not screenshots or evidence of success.

steps.title: Roll back safely when a check fails
steps.where: APP01 · IIS Manager, recovery record and isolated lab
actions: Stop PracticeHelpdesk first and record the failed check and new errors. Keep the candidate folder/logs for investigation. Do not restore a whole-VM checkpoint or overwrite the database as the first response to a PHP mapping problem.

Check the previous runtime against the security advisory BEFORE putting it back into service. If it is older than the fixed minimum or otherwise vulnerable, leave the live pool stopped. Investigate that old runtime only on an isolated copy with no user traffic, or repair the patched candidate. Availability is not permission to reopen vulnerable PHP.

If the previous runtime is still security-approved, select this site → Handler Mappings → PHP-FastCGI → Edit and restore its recorded previous executable. Restore only its recorded candidate-specific FastCGI/environment settings and the previous protected php.ini if those were changed. Do not remove an entry used by another website.

Restart only this pool and repeat the web-served version and every acceptance check. Reopen only when the old runtime remains patched and the application passes. Otherwise stop it again and keep a maintenance notice or unavailable service.

A PHP-only mapping rollback normally does not need a database restore. If application/schema/data changes also occurred, stop and use a separately approved application-consistent restore plan; restoring an older database can erase new tickets. Restore server-wide IIS configuration only after checking the effect on every site.
Record the rollback decision, exact runtime/configuration restored, ticket/data checks and next corrective action. Never mark a failed patch successful merely because you rolled back.
steps.expected: The app is either healthy on a security-approved runtime or remains unavailable pending a safe fix. No vulnerable runtime was returned to service.

screenshot.title: Roll back safely when a check fails
screenshot.instructions: Compare the written actions with your own practice machine. Diagrams are not screenshots or evidence of success.

steps.title: Follow the error to the right component
steps.where: APP01 · IIS Manager → PracticeHelpdesk → Logging
actions: Find the site ID and its log folder, normally C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC<site-id>. Make one failed request and match its timestamp, path, status and substatus.

For 404, check URL, physical path and index.php. For 403, check default document, authorization and file permissions. For 500, check PHP configuration and logs; 500.19 often points to invalid configuration or a missing module.
For 502.3, investigate FastCGI startup, runtime architecture and PHP errors. Recycle only this pool after a fix. Do not disable all security or restart every website.
steps.expected: You can match a real request to its IIS log record and a targeted next check.

actions: Use the Nessus classes to create a scan scoped only to APP01’s recorded private address. Resolve helpdesk.lab.example.test through your lab DNS; do not scan the public lab.example.test address by accident.
Set a light practice scan, record permission/scope, and compare findings with the installed versions and actual settings. Keep availability checks and backup ready.
Fix one verified issue, repeat the same scan and test ticket creation. A clean scan alone does not prove the application is secure. Nessus on Windows uses its own service, not IIS.
steps.expected: The scan scope is private APP01, findings are reviewed, and the app still works afterward.

steps.title: Record the Azure migration baseline

actions: Record the Server 2019 version, PHP/osTicket/MariaDB versions, help desk URL, ticket ID, attachment test, certificate expiry, backup path and database size.

Follow the existing Azure migration lessons to move the VMware workload to a supported private Azure network and check it before the Server 2022 upgrade. Use a supported migration/upgrade procedure for the exact VM and OS; keep rollback available.

At cutover, point the PRIVATE helpdesk.lab.example.test A record at the validated Azure private address reachable from your lab/client network. Do not edit a guest’s static IP as though it were an Azure NIC setting. Re-test HTTPS, login, a ticket, attachment, mail and backup.
